title: English 10
description: Explore novels, poetry, drama, and essays. Develop close reading analysis, build interpretations with evidence, and sharpen your thinking through discussion.

items.title: Novel
items.summary: Read sustained narratives and related non-fiction through authorial choices, evidence, and discussion.
items.body:
## Reading focus
Explore how writers shape character, conflict, perspective, and larger ideas through language and structure. The 2026–27 syllabus pairs William Golding's *Lord of the Flies* with selected non-fiction, including survival writing and other related texts.

## Notice and interpret
Follow recurring images, changes in relationships, contrasts, and moments when objects or actions acquire significance. Test interpretations against the surrounding passage and the wider text.

## Reading notes
Keep a dialectical journal or equivalent notes: a precise reference, an observation about a choice, a possible interpretation, and a question worth discussing.

## Put the reading to work
Develop short close reading analyses of fiction and non-fiction. Bring evidence and open questions to a Socratic seminar. The task sheet specifies the current focus and level of support.

items.title: Poetry
items.summary: Read voice, imagery, sound, and form; explain how patterns and shifts shape meaning.
items.body:
## Reading focus
Read a range of poets, voices, and forms. Establish the literal situation before exploring implications. Distinguish the speaker from the poet.

## Notice and interpret
Examine the interaction of imagery, diction, rhythm, sound, line breaks, and stanza structure. Look for shifts and patterns that develop a reading rather than collecting devices.

## Put the reading to work
Write CRAs on seen and unseen poems. Develop a poem presentation that explains choices with evidence and responds to questions from classmates. Experiments in writing poetry can help you notice what formal choices make possible.

## Another way in
If you need a sequence of reading prompts, try [TPCASTT](/courses/literature/resources/81a5570b-6369-4557-b98b-9d8fa1be2f52). Use it to generate observations, then select the ones that help answer the task.

items.title: Drama
items.summary: Explore how dialogue, staging, and performance turn a script into an interpretation.
items.body:
## Reading focus
Study dramatic structure, character relationships, and the possibilities of performance. The 2026–27 syllabus includes Shakespeare's *Romeo and Juliet* and Baz Luhrmann's 1996 film adaptation, *Romeo + Juliet*.

## Notice and interpret
Track what characters say, what they conceal, and how their words affect each other. Consider stage directions, delivery, movement, and relationships in space. In film, examine framing, image composition, and other choices that shape a scene.

## Put the reading to work
Compare a particular moment in the script with its interpretation in performance or film. Develop image-analysis CRAs and a speaking/listening multimedia task. Explain the effect of a choice rather than judging an adaptation only by its fidelity to the script.

items.title: Essay
items.summary: Examine personal voice and perspective, then make deliberate choices in your own writing.
items.body:
## Reading focus
Read personal essays to explore how writers make experience meaningful for a reader. Attend to voice, perspective, tone, and the relationship between a particular event and a larger reflection.

## Notice and interpret
Examine word choice, selection of detail, sentence patterns, and structure. Ask how the writer moves between recounting an experience and reflecting on it.

## Put the reading to work
Develop a CRA explaining how choices shape meaning and voice. Experiment with those choices in your own personal writing. The syllabus includes a college-application essay exercise; use the prompt supplied for the current task.

items.title: Close reading analysis (CRA)
items.summary: Move from a guided analytical paragraph to independent, connected analysis.
items.body:
## The task
A CRA explains how an author's choices shape meaning in a short passage or other assigned text. Responses may address seen or unseen material and are often timed. Across the course, tasks develop toward responses of roughly 250–500 words; follow the word limit and paragraph requirements on each task sheet.

## How the support changes
### 1. A supplied focus
Work with a technique or focus selected by your teacher. Learn to choose precise evidence and explain its effects in one coherent paragraph.

### 2. Your choice
Select a significant authorial choice yourself. Explain why it matters to the passage, rather than picking a device simply because you can name it.

### 3. A connected response
Develop several related choices across paragraphs when the task calls for it. Give each paragraph a clear purpose and connect it to the overall interpretation.

## Build the paragraph
- Begin with a thesis that answers the prompt and offers an interpretation.
- Select short quotations that let you examine particular words or phrases closely.
- Explain meanings and associations in context.
- Show how the choices work together to shape meaning.
- Link your ideas logically and close by drawing the interpretation together.

## An early task format
The CRA 2.0 practice on Sebastian Junger's *The Perfect Storm* asks how the author's words and phrases shape meaning. It requires **one well-organized paragraph of no more than 250 words**, a clear thesis, short quotations, and a concluding sentence in a formal academic register. That limit belongs to this task; it is not a universal CRA limit.

## Check your analysis
Does the evidence support the interpretation? Have you explained the quoted language rather than retold the passage? Are the choices connected? Can you replace a vague effect such as “creates an image” with a more precise explanation?

## Practice
Use the [close reading lab](/courses/english-10/practice/754594bb-c1ef-45bc-953c-5655a2b25ac9) to develop a reading, then the [paragraph workshop](/courses/english-10/practice/62b095f4-b49c-4f4f-ab8a-9dfa3348649a) to organize it. Check the rubric supplied with the task for the assessed reading, writing, and language strands.

items.title: Socratic seminar
items.summary: Develop a reading through evidence, questions, and thoughtful responses to others.
items.body:
## Prepare
Read and annotate the assigned text. Bring a few precise references, an interpretation you can explain, and open questions that invite more than a factual answer. Use your reading notes or dialectical journal to trace both observations and uncertainties.

## Contribute
Make a claim, locate the supporting detail, and explain the connection. Keep contributions focused enough to leave room for others to respond.

## Listen and develop
Build on an idea, question its evidence, offer another reading, or connect two contributions. Refer to what a classmate actually said. You may revise your interpretation as the discussion develops.

## Avoid
- Rehearsing a speech while someone else is speaking.
- Repeating a claim without adding evidence or reasoning.
- Treating participation as a count of how often you speak.
- Disagreeing with a person rather than examining an interpretation.

## Reflect
Record an idea that changed or became more precise. Identify the evidence or contribution that helped, then set one goal for the next discussion. Follow the seminar's specific task sheet and rubric.

items.title: From observation to analysis
items.summary: A short guide to building interpretations with evidence.
items.body:
## Start with a precise observation
What word, image, pattern, or structural choice catches your attention? Quote briefly and accurately.

## Explore a possible effect
How might that choice shape a reader’s response? Consider the context before making a claim about its effect.

## Connect detail to meaning
Explain how the evidence supports your interpretation. A useful starting phrase is: “This choice suggests … because …”

## Test your interpretation
Can you find a second detail that supports your reading? Is there evidence that complicates it? Revise your idea if necessary.

items.title: Close reading lab
items.summary: Notice a choice. Develop an interpretation. Explain its effect.
items.body:
## Before you begin
Choose a short passage from a text you are studying. Use the prompts below to develop an interpretation supported by precise details.

items.title: Paragraph workshop
items.summary: Connect your claim, evidence, and analysis.
items.body:
## Build a purposeful paragraph
Work with a passage from your current text. Your goal is to explain how a particular choice creates meaning, rather than simply naming a technique.
